title: Luke 15:17 - Coming to your senses
series: The Lamp and the Word [CHECK: series name - the recording says 'The Lamp and the Word', the plan says 'Faith in Motion']

clips._note: 81.2-87.8 is a first take ('Sunday's episode...'); the retake below is used instead

captions.t: Have you ever had a moment where you suddenly saw your life clearly?
Just... click.
And you thought, "What am I doing?"
There's a verse in the story of the prodigal son that describes exactly that moment.
It's only one line long,
captions.check: heard as 'It's not only one line long'

captions.t: but I think it might be one of the most hopeful sentences in the whole Bible.
Welcome to The Lamp and the Word.
Today we're spending five minutes on one verse.
Luke 15:17.
If you watched the last video, which happens to be our first video,
you know the story.
A young man demands his inheritance early,
leaves home, and wastes everything.
A famine hits. He ends up feeding pigs.
And he's so hungry that even the pigs' food looks good to him.
He has hit the very bottom.
And then Jesus says this:
"When he finally came to his senses, he said to himself,
'At home, even the hired servants have food enough to spare,
and here I am dying of hunger!
I will go home to my father.'"
When he finally came to his senses.
Some translations say, "when he came to himself."
It's as if, all this time,
captions.check: heard as 'It's a safe. all this time.'

captions.t: he had been living as someone he wasn't.
And in that pig field, he finally woke up.
Look closely at that verse and you will see three things happen inside him.
First: he tells himself the truth.
"Here I am dying of hunger."
No excuses. No blaming the famine,
or his friends, or his father.
For the first time, he stops pretending he's fine.
And that's where every real change begins.
Not when we feel guilty.
We can feel guilty for years and change nothing.
Change begins when we finally stop lying to ourselves about where we are.
Second: he remembers his father's house.
Notice what brings him back.
It isn't the pigs. It's a memory.
"At home, even the servants have food enough to spare."
He remembers that his father is generous,
that there is more than enough in that house.
And friends, that is what draws us home to God too.
Not fear, but His goodness.
captions.check: heard as 'not fearfest. But it's goodness.'

captions.t: Romans chapter 2 says it is God's kindness that leads us to repentance.
The son came to his senses because he remembered what his father was like.
Third: he gets up.
"I will go home to my father."
Coming to your senses isn't just a feeling.
It turns into a decision, and the decision turns into steps.
He still has the dirt on his clothes.
He still has a speech he's practicing: "Make me a hired servant."
He doesn't have it all figured out.
He just starts walking.
And here's the part that undoes me.
Every time, it strikes me. Every time.
captions.check: possible stumble or retake; listen and keep or cut 126.5-129.3

captions.t: When he finally gets close to home,
he never even gets to finish his speech,
because the father is already running toward him.
The son came to his senses.
But the father had never lost his.
He had been watching that road the whole time.
So maybe you're watching this from your own pig field.
Maybe it's a habit you swore you'd never go back to.
A relationship that's pulling you away from God.
Or maybe it's quieter than that.
You're still in church, but your heart wandered off a long time ago.
Here is the good news of Luke 15:17:
you don't have to clean yourself up before you come home.
You only have to come to your senses.
Tell yourself the truth. Acknowledge the truth.
captions.check: 'Acknowledge the truth' may be a second take of 'Tell yourself the truth'

captions.t: Remember what your Father is like, and take the first step toward Him.
And if you're not sure what that first step is,
it can be as simple as praying this with me, right where you are.
Father, I've been far from You.
I'm done pretending I'm fine.
Thank You that Your house is full of grace,
and that You have been watching the road for me.
I'm coming home.
Thank You for running to meet me.
In Jesus' name, amen.
If you prayed that, I would love to know.
Just type "I'm coming home" in the comments, and I'll be praying for you by name this week.
If you haven't seen the full story yet,
the last episode walks through the whole parable, including the older brother,
and he might surprise you.
I'll put it right here.
See you next time.

beats.desc: Close-up: a young man's tired, dirty face, eyes slowly lifting. The moment it clicks.
Wide: the same man sitting in a muddy pig pen at dusk.
Ancient countryside at golden hour: fields, hills, a pig field in the distance.
The father's house in an ancient village, warm evening light.
The young man walking away from home down a road with a money pouch; the father in the doorway.
Wasting everything: coins spilling, a party fading (tasteful).
Famine: cracked dry earth, an empty market.
Feeding pigs, hungry, staring at the pods in the trough.
Rain or dusk in the pig field; he sits in the mud, head down.

beats.title: When he finally came to his senses, he said to himself, “At home even the hired servants have food enough to spare, and here I am dying of hunger! I will go home to my father…”
beats.check: translation: wording matches NLT; confirm that's the one Niqui reads

beats.desc: Slow push-in on his face as his eyes open. Realisation.
He looks at his reflection in a puddle or water trough.
He rises slowly to his feet; light breaks through the clouds.
He looks at his empty hands and torn clothes. Honest, no excuses.
Today: a person alone by a window at night, thinking (a modern parallel).
Memory, soft and dreamlike: a warm table full of bread, servants laughing.
The father at the gate, kind face, looking down the road.

beats.title: God's kindness leads us to repentance.

beats.desc: The son's face softens as he remembers.
He stands and turns toward the road home.
Walking a long dirt road in dusty clothes, mouthing his speech.
A small figure far down the road; the father in the distance sees him.
The father running toward his son, robes flying.
The embrace.
The father on the rooftop at sunrise, watching the road (the whole time).
Today: someone sitting on the edge of a bed at night, phone light on their face.
A church pew; someone present but far away in their thoughts.
Sunrise over a road that leads home.
